"* This paragraph describes how the writer Jeffrey Eugenides once said that the more you learn about your country, the more ashamed you can feel, just like when you learn more about yourself. He wrote this line back in 2005, before big events like Hurricane Katrina, the housing crisis, and the election of a TV star as president. The article suggests that America’s problems seem even worse now, and the interviewer asks if national shame is bigger than personal shame. Eugenides replies that they are about equal, because everyone has a past that includes troubling things like slavery. He hints that both personal and national histories contain pain, and that this “inventory” of shame never really ends. He says that at the moment people might focus more on national issues, but personal problems and national problems are closely linked. This shows the tension between feeling bad about what the country has done and what individuals have done. He believes a nation is just a collection of people, so national problems are really personal problems too. The passage wants to highlight how hard it is to separate your own conscience from your country’s behavior.

* The scene then shifts to Eugenides speaking in a nearly finished university building at Princeton, where he has taught for 10 years. The unfinished building has a simple paper sign that says “unisex” on the bathroom door, which shows how cultural attitudes have changed in a short time. This small detail acts as a quiet welcome to people who do not fit strict gender categories. It also shows that campus life has become more aware of identity, bodies, and health issues linked to gender. The article reminds us that when Eugenides toured with his novel Middlesex years ago, he often had to explain what “intersex” meant, because many people had never heard the term. Now, ideas about gender are more visible and widely discussed. This change reflects broader social shifts in America during the last decade. There is still tension between old ways of thinking and new understandings of identity. The passage uses this setting, and even that simple bathroom sign, to highlight how both the country and its people keep changing. It quietly suggests that these social changes affect not just the public world, but also private relationships, like how someone might talk about identity with a girlfriend or a friend.*"
